title: The UK and the EU need an economic security partnership
gist: Chatham House argues the 20 November 2026 UK–EU reset summit should launch a structured economic security partnership against coercion, Chinese overcapacity, an unpredictable US and supply shocks. Since tariff and 'Made in Europe' alignment is politically hard, it should start with information-sharing between the UK's Investment Security Unit and EU screening authorities on high-risk (including Chinese) investment, later expanding to supply-chain early warning and anti-coercion coordination.

insights.claim: The second UK–EU 'reset' summit on 20 November 2026 was delayed six months to let prime minister Andy Burnham's new government set priorities, and is expected to complete Starmer-era deals on SPS checks, a youth experience scheme and linking the UK and EU emissions trading systems.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch the summit outcome for ETS linkage, which would affect UK carbon allowance pricing convergence with EU allowances.
insights.locator: The second UK–EU ‘reset’ summit takes place on 20 November

insights.claim: The UK government estimates the UK–EU sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement, which removes most checks on trade in animals, plants and their products, could eventually be worth £5.1 billion a year.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: UK agrifood exporters and cross-Channel logistics are the direct beneficiaries if the SPS deal is completed.
insights.quote: the UK government estimates the SPS deal could eventually be worth £5.1 billion a year
insights.locator: Completing these agreements is important for growth

insights.claim: Chatham House argues the Burnham government should make economic security — protecting sensitive assets, withstanding coercion and supply shocks, and building strategic capabilities — a central pillar of a more strategic UK–EU partnership beyond trade and mobility deals.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals a policy shift from tariff/mobility deals toward security-driven coordination on investment, supply chains and coercion.
insights.locator: But the Burnham government will likely also want a more strategic partnership

insights.claim: The EU's 'Made in Europe' initiatives, chiefly the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, favour European-made products in public procurement and subsidy schemes and risk shutting UK firms out of European supply chains unless UK goods receive equal treatment.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: UK industrials selling into EU procurement and subsidy-backed supply chains face exclusion risk pending a decision on UK treatment.

insights.claim: The EU decision on whether UK firms will be covered by 'Made in Europe' rules appears to have been pushed into 2027, leaving UK suppliers' status unresolved.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Prolonged uncertainty for UK exporters dependent on EU procurement; the decision is a 2027 catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: For now, the decision over ‘Made in Europe’ appears to have been kicked into next year.
insights.locator: For now, the decision over ‘Made in Europe’

insights.claim: The EU is wary of extending subsidy and procurement benefits to the UK without reciprocal access to UK schemes and UK alignment on tariffs and investment conditions towards China, while the UK will resist overt rule-taking or limits on its trade-policy freedom.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: 'Made in Europe' access for UK firms likely requires the UK to harden its China tariff and investment stance — a trade-off with UK–China commerce.
insights.locator: However, while political will is growing on both sides

insights.claim: Since Brexit the global economy has become far more adversarial: the US uses tariffs as bargaining chips and China restricts exports of critical inputs such as rare earths to advance geopolitical goals.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Supports structural premium for non-Chinese rare-earth and critical-input supply and for supply-chain resilience spending.
insights.locator: Since Brexit, the global economy has become far more adversarial.

insights.claim: Chatham House argues middle powers such as the UK, Australia, Canada, Japan and South Korea must cooperate to manage geo-economic pressure, but the EU is the UK's most consequential economic security partner due to proximity, integrated supply chains and shared security interests.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect middle-power coordination (supply-chain, critical minerals) to become a policy bloc that shapes trade flows outside US–China.
insights.quote: the EU is the UK’s most consequential economic security partner, due to its proximity, integrated supply chains and shared security interests

insights.claim: The UK and EU share exposure to coercion, Chinese overcapacity and an unpredictable US, as well as common dependencies in critical minerals, energy and some advanced technologies.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Joint UK–EU action on Chinese overcapacity (e.g. trade defence) becomes more likely as shared vulnerabilities are formalised.

insights.claim: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz triggered an energy price crisis, cited as the type of geo-economic shock a UK–EU partnership should jointly address with like-minded partners.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Energy supply shocks are being folded into economic-security policy, supporting coordinated stockpiling and energy-security measures.
insights.quote: the energy price crisis that followed the closure of the Strait of Hormuz
insights.locator: It should also consider ways to jointly engage

insights.claim: Chatham House proposes a UK–EU economic security partnership built on existing structures — the 2021 Trade and Cooperation Agreement Partnership Council, the 2025 Security and Defence Partnership and annual summits — with an annual ministerial dialogue and official-level working groups comparing geo-economic risk assessments including on China.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Institutionalised UK–EU risk assessment on China would raise policy alignment odds on overcapacity and investment screening.
insights.locator: This partnership could build on existing structures.

insights.claim: The partnership should include an upfront commitment to consult on responses if either side faces retaliation for joint measures, for example if the UK aligns with EU tariffs or investment conditions on Chinese goods or capital to secure 'Made in Europe' treatment.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Anticipates Chinese retaliation risk against UK if it aligns with EU China measures — a tail risk for UK firms with China exposure.
insights.locator: From the outset, the partnership should also include a commitment to consult

insights.claim: Aligning UK and EU tariffs and industrial policy is hard because they compete in some industrial sectors and for investment, and because the UK sits outside the single market and cannot use the EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument ('trade bazooka').
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Do not expect quick UK–EU tariff alignment; near-term cooperation will be in lower-cost protective tools.

insights.claim: Chatham House argues cooperation on investment risks, research security and critical supply-chain vulnerabilities carries lower political and economic costs than tariff alignment and plays to UK strengths, since the UK and EU currently share too little information in these areas.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Investment screening coordination is the likeliest near-term deliverable, raising scrutiny on Chinese-linked deals in both markets.
insights.quote: At present, the UK and the EU share too little information on investment risks, research security and vulnerabilities in critical supply chains.
insights.locator: At present, the UK and the EU share too little information

insights.claim: The UK's National Security and Investment Act is one of Europe's more developed screening regimes, while the EU only recently made national-security investment screening mandatory for all member states.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Tighter, more uniform screening across Europe increases deal-approval risk for sensitive-sector M&A involving Chinese capital.
insights.locator: The UK’s National Security and Investment Act (NSIA)

insights.claim: A practical first step would be an information-sharing arrangement between the UK's Investment Security Unit and EU member states' screening authorities to address high-risk investments, including from China.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Shared intelligence on high-risk investors would make Chinese bids for UK/EU sensitive assets (data, tech, IP) harder to clear.

insights.claim: Once trust is built, the UK and EU should establish a joint supply-chain disruption early-warning system modelled on the US-Japan-South Korea system, linking the UK's Supply Chain Centre with the EU's critical-goods monitoring.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Earlier detection of supply disruptions could dampen shock-driven price spikes in critical goods.

insights.claim: Within two years the partnership should create a channel for coordinating responses to coercion, including how the UK's emerging anti-coercion framework works alongside the EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument, and over the long term foster strategic industrial collaboration pooling resources and talent.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A coordinated UK–EU anti-coercion posture would raise the cost of trade coercion by China or the US against either.
